Gimme Some Skin
GIM-ee sum SKIN
phrase (Boomer slang)
Jazz and jive talk of the 1930s–40s: give me some skin or slip me some skin, a request for a friendly hand slap or handshake, palm against palm, as a greeting, congratulation, or seal of agreement. It passed into 1950s–60s Black and hipster slang, was used by Boomer teens, and gave rise to give me five, low five, and finally the high five of the late 1970s.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Gimme some skin means "slap my hand" — a hip handshake, palm sliding across palm, for hello, congratulations, or "it’s a deal." It is the ancestor of the high five. The Christian observation: Scripture knows the meaning of a hand given, and it knows both its warmth and its weight. The warmth: when Jehu met Jehonadab on the road, he asked, "Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart? And Jehonadab answered, It is. If it be, give me thine hand. And he gave him his hand" (2Ki 10:15). The apostles gave Paul "the right hands of fellowship" (Gal 2:9). A hand given is a heart pledged; that is why a handshake once meant more than a contract. The weight: Proverbs warns that striking hands can bind a man to another’s debts. "My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger" (Pro 6:1), deliver yourself; "Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts" (Pro 22:26). The slap of agreement is a promise, and promises bind. So a Christian can give some skin freely in greeting and joy, and carefully in business. And the deepest word about skin and hands in Scripture belongs to Christ, whose hands were pierced to seal the covenant that saves — "a friend loveth at all times" (Pro 17:17), and He is that Friend.

Webster 1828 Definition

1930s–40s jive talk, carried into Boomer slang, for a palm-slap handshake of greeting or agreement, ancestor of the high five — a hand given is a heart pledged (2Ki 10:15), and a hand struck can bind (Pro 6:1).

expand to see more

GIMME SOME SKIN, phr. (jazz / jive slang, 1930s–40s; Boomer-era use) Give me a hand slap or handshake, as a greeting, congratulation, or sign of agreement. Also slip me some skin, give me five.

Webster (1828) — SKIN, noun 1. The natural covering of animal bodies, consisting of the cuticle or scarf-skin, the rete mucosum, and the cutis or hide. The cuticle is very thin and insensible; the cutis is thicker and very sensible. 2. A hide; a pelt; the skin of an animal separated from the body, whether green, dry or tanned.

Decode for families: before the high five there was skin. Before skin, there was the handshake that meant "my word is good."

Key Scripture

2Ki 10:15 — "And when he was departed thence, he lighted on Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him: and he saluted him, and said to him, Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart? And Jehonadab answered, It is. If it be, give me thine hand. And he gave him his hand; and he took him up to him into the chariot."

Gal 2:9 — "And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision."

Pro 6:1 — "My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger,"

Pro 22:26 — "Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts."

Pro 17:17 — "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity."

Modern Corruption

A friendly, harmless gesture; Scripture adds that a hand given pledges the heart and that a hand struck in agreement can bind, so it should be given freely in friendship and carefully in debt.

expand to see more

There is nothing sinful in a hand slap, and the jive-era greeting carried a real warmth among friends who had little else to give each other. The only lesson Scripture adds is about the weight of the hand. In the ancient world, as in many places still, striking hands sealed an agreement, and Proverbs warns young men again and again not to strike hands as surety for others’ debts. A culture that has turned the handshake into a casual gesture may have lost the sense that a man’s word, sealed by his hand, should be good.

The warm side of the gesture is Jehu’s question: "Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart?" (2Ki 10:15). That is what every true greeting asks. A Christian who gives some skin to a brother is, in a small way, giving the right hand of fellowship (Gal 2:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old Norse skinn (hide) → English skin; 1930s–40s jive give / slip me some skin → 1950s–60s give me five → late-1970s high five.
